summary: A magazine spread that happens to be a web page. Type carries the voice; the image only sets the room.
source: Tilda Editorial Style · UX Planet §10 (Luxury Typography), §33 (Mixed Media)

accent.role: one editorial red, on kickers and pull quotes ONLY

type.ratioNote: 46px display against 14px body. THIS IS THE STYLE'S CORE MOVE.

focus.reason: the editorial red is already reserved for kickers and pull quotes, so it reads as 'the marked thing' — which is exactly what a focus ring is. 5.9:1 on paper.

motion.note: print has no hover. Keep it to a link underline.

copyBudget.measureColumns: 34-44ch per column when using CSS columns
copyBudget.headlineReason: the ONLY pack that raises the engine's limit — a magazine deck is a sentence, not a label
copyBudget.note: the HIGHEST budget in the catalogue. This style exists to be READ; the engine's 420 would gut it.

a11y.note: long-form body text at 17px/1.6 on warm paper is the most readable configuration in the catalogue. The risk here is not contrast, it is MEASURE.
a11y.targetSizeNote: Small-caps section labels are this pack's target-size risk: 11px uppercase renders under 24px tall. Nav links carry padding plus min-height:25px.
a11y.assetRule: ROUTER Gate 2.5 — imagery is a RASTER, never CSS. page.html ships a declared placeholder (data-asset='...-pending') with a flat fill, which engine/audit.mjs fails on until the real photograph lands. A gradient stand-in would break the pack's own ban as well.
a11y.measureRule: Editorial's measure is 58-70ch and that is a pack rule, not a per-element choice. It is declared once at main p and elements only tighten it. Widening the page from 1080 to 1320 pushed an uncapped paragraph to 95ch — proof that a measure inherited from the container is not a measure at all.

banned: cards — editorial content sits on the page, not in containers
rounded corners and shadows on imagery
a single type size for headings and body — it kills the contrast that defines the style
sans-serif body text at long measure

darkMode.note: Warm paper inverts to warm near-black #17150f, not neutral. A cold grey dark mode makes serif body text look like a terminal. Ink becomes #ece7dd.

scroll.headline: scrollytelling (●)
scroll.reason: this style IS long-form narrative. Scrollytelling is not an effect bolted on — the sticky image with text scrolling beside it is literally a magazine spread.
banned: scroll-snap — snapping fights reading, and this style exists to be read

sheet.metaLine: warm paper #faf7f2 · display:body ≥ 3:1 · serif body 17/1.6 · one red
tokenTable: 46px display vs 14px body — the core move

notes.tokens: Display-to-body ratio is the whole style. Everything else follows from committing to at least 3:1 — a 46px display against 14px body. Match the sizes and you have a blog, not a spread.
notes.nav: A masthead: the title at scale, a rule under it, and small-caps section labels. No bar, no fill. This is the one pack where the header is typography rather than chrome.
notes.hero: A deck, not a headline — the only pack that raises the engine's 8-word limit, to 9, because a magazine deck is a sentence. The kicker above it does the work an eyebrow does elsewhere.
notes.button: Editorial barely has buttons. The primary is a solid ink block; secondary is a ruled link. Focus uses the editorial red, which already means the marked thing in this pack's vocabulary.
notes.form: A subscribe field — the only form a magazine has. Ruled underline, serif input text, error as a red rule plus a line of italic.
notes.card: There is no card, and that ban is load-bearing. The specimen shows the alternative: content separated by a column rule and space. A card grid is the exact opposite of an editorial spread.
notes.table: Ruled rows, no fills, serif figures. Tabular numerals matter here — font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums keeps a column of figures aligned in a proportional serif.
notes.overlay: A paper panel over a warm scrim. No radius, no shadow — the panel is identified by the rule at its head, like a sidebar in print.
notes.empty: A kicker, a line of italic, one action. Editorial has a natural vocabulary for absence: the standfirst that says what would have been here.
notes.dark: Warm paper inverts to warm near-black #17150f, not neutral grey. A cold dark mode makes serif body text read like a terminal.
notes.narrow: Two columns collapse to one and the measure caps at 62ch. The display size drops but the 3:1 ratio does not — that ratio is the style, and it is the first thing lost on mobile.
notes.copy: 900 chars per viewport — the highest in the catalogue, against the engine's 420. This style exists to be read; the default budget would gut it.

Long read · Issue 04

The grid is an argument, not a container

By A. Reyes · 14 min · Photographs by M. Okafor

Nine words in the deck — the only pack here that raises the engine's eight-word ceiling, because a magazine deck is a sentence rather than a label, and the body runs at seventeen pixels on a sixty-four character measure.

Fig. 1 — Declared placeholder (data-asset="…-pending"). ROUTER Gate 2.5: a photograph is a raster, never CSS. The image sets the room; it does not carry the argument.

01 — The ratio

Contrast is the whole trick

A forty-six pixel display against fourteen pixel body, set on warm paper rather than white. Match the sizes and you have a blog.

Type carries the voice; the image only sets the room.

There is no card here and there will not be one. Editorial content sits on the page, separated by a column rule and by space, exactly as it does in print — which is why the ban on cards is load-bearing rather than stylistic.

Scrollytelling is not an effect bolted onto this style. The sticky image with text moving beside it is literally a spread, which is why it is the one technique rated core here and why snap is banned: snapping fights reading.

Everything above has been one column of continuous prose at a fixed measure. That is the test — if the layout cannot hold a long argument, it is not editorial.

The column has to be substantially taller than the figure beside it, or the pin lasts a second and the technique reads as a glitch. That is a composition requirement, not a CSS one: scrollytelling needs enough text to scroll past.

A pin that does not hold is worse than no pin.

Warm paper rather than white, ink at #141414 rather than pure black, and a serif set at seventeen pixels on a 1.6 leading. None of that is decoration — it is the configuration that makes long-form text comfortable to read.

The kicker above each section does the work an eyebrow does elsewhere, and the pull quote breaks the column without breaking the measure. Both are print devices, and both survive the move to a screen unchanged.

When the figure finally releases, it should be because the argument has finished — not because the container ran out.
